title: Training a Coding Model to Paint: RL Where the Reward Is How the Output Looks
hook: The model writes JavaScript; the environment runs it in a headless browser, renders the painting, and scores the picture. A worked example of RL over an aesthetic, non-textual reward.
key_points: Task: get Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to write p5.brush JavaScript that renders watercolour hibiscus paintings.
OpenEnv wraps the whole loop — p5.brush, headless Chromium rendering, and reward computation — as an RL environment.
TRL's GRPO trainer with LoRA adapters does the training; the reward never touches the code's text, only the rendered image.
Composite reward: a validity gate, code length, pairwise visual comparison against a pool of 178 hand-rated paintings, and the HPSv3 aesthetic preference model.
Reward improved +0.13 to +0.27 across three runs; the pairwise-judge runs doubled paint coverage versus the model-only baseline.
Cost was roughly 18 hours per 60 steps on an H200.
content_html: Reinforcement learning on code usually means rewards you can check with a test suite. Paniego's post — reproducing an idea from Surya Narreddi — pushes the loop somewhere stranger: the model, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, writes JavaScript using the p5.brush library, and the reward comes from looking at the watercolour painting that code produces.
extra_html:
How it works

OpenEnv wraps the whole pipeline as an RL environment: run the generated code, render it headless in Chromium, and compute a score. Training uses TRL's GRPO trainer with LoRA adapters. The composite reward mixes a validity gate (0.05), a code-length term (0.05), pairwise visual comparison against a pool of 178 hand-rated paintings generated by four open models (0.30–0.60), and the HPSv3 aesthetic preference model (0.30–0.60), with the weights varied across runs.

Why it matters

Three runs — hps-only at 60 steps, judge-led and hps-led at 110 — improved reward by +0.13, +0.27, and +0.24 respectively, and the pairwise-judge runs doubled paint coverage compared with the model-only baseline. Roughly 18 hours per 60 steps on an H200 is a useful anchor for what environment-heavy RL costs. Beyond the pretty pictures, this is a template: when your objective is only expressible by running the output and looking at the result, you can put the renderer inside the training loop.

flashcards.prompt: What makes this reward signal unusual for a code-generation task?
flashcards.back_html: Nothing is scored on the code itself — the environment executes it, renders the image in headless Chromium, and judges the picture's appearance.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the reward combine a pairwise visual judge against a curated pool with an aesthetic preference model, rather than using one alone?

choices.text: Each covers a different failure mode — relative quality against real examples, and absolute aesthetic preference
The preference model is too slow to run on every rollout
Pairwise comparison is only used to break ties in the final ranking

flashcards.explanation_html: The run variants show the mix matters: judge-led training improved reward most (+0.27) and the pairwise-judge runs doubled paint coverage compared with the model-only baseline.

flashcards.prompt: What role does OpenEnv play here?
flashcards.back_html: It packages the p5.brush library, headless Chromium rendering, and reward computation into a single RL environment the TRL GRPO trainer can step through.
